nodes.title: Determinants and nonvanishing
nodes.summary: A determinant detects whether a square matrix is invertible.
nodes.detail: For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det=ad−bc. Nonzero determinant means the associated linear system has a unique solution for every right-hand side.
nodes.proof: If ad−bc≠0, multiplying the matrix by [[d,−b],[−c,a]] gives (ad−bc)I. Dividing gives an inverse. For [[1,2],[3,4]], det=−2≠0.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Prime valuations of rational numbers
nodes.summary: v_p(q) counts the exponent of a prime p in a nonzero rational q.
nodes.detail: Write q as a ratio of integers and subtract denominator exponents from numerator exponents. Negative valuations mean powers of p in the denominator.
nodes.proof: For q=12/5=2²·3·5⁻¹, v₂(q)=2, v₃(q)=1, and v₅(q)=−1. Unique prime factorization gives v_p(ab)=v_p(a)+v_p(b) for nonzero rationals a,b.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: The product formula over rational numbers
nodes.summary: The ordinary size of a nonzero rational balances all its prime-based sizes.
nodes.detail: Define |q|_p=p^(−v_p(q)). For nonzero rational q, |q| times the product of |q|_p over all primes is one; only finitely many factors differ from one.
nodes.proof: Write q=±∏p p^eₚ. Then |q|=∏p p^eₚ and ∏p|q|_p=∏p p^(−eₚ). Multiplying cancels each exponent. This elementary identity does not establish the manuscript’s estimates for each prime.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Logarithms turn products into sums
nodes.summary: Logarithms let us compare multiplicative growth using additive estimates.
nodes.detail: For positive a,b, log(ab)=log a+log b. A real logarithm requires a strictly positive argument, so log|Δ| requires Δ≠0.
nodes.proof: If a_N=e^(−cN²), then log(a_N)/N²=−c. Normalizing a logarithm can expose the rate hidden in a very small number. This is an example, not an estimate for the manuscript determinants.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Upper and lower limits
nodes.summary: Limsup and liminf record eventual upper and lower behavior even without convergence.
nodes.detail: For a bounded sequence x_n, take the supremum and infimum of each tail, then let the tail move outward.
nodes.proof: For x_n=(−1)^n+1/n, even terms tend to 1 and odd terms tend to −1. Thus limsup=1 and liminf=−1: a sequence can have bounds without a single limit.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Why the Catalan argument needs two estimates
nodes.summary: The source compares arithmetic and analytic bounds for the same nonzero determinants.
nodes.detail: The arithmetic side uses rationality, prime valuations, and a product formula. The analytic side estimates the real size. Normalized logarithms put both on a common scale. Each source estimate remains a separate unverified research claim.
nodes.proof: The final numerical comparison is elementary: −2.29084 exceeds −2.2909 by 0.00006. If the claimed lower and upper limits hold for the same real sequence, they contradict liminf≤limsup. The hard work is establishing those estimates.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Matrix multiplication as composition
nodes.summary: Matrix multiplication combines two linear transformations.
nodes.detail: If A is m×k and B is k×n, then (AB)ᵢⱼ=Σₗ Aᵢₗ Bₗⱼ. Matching inner dimensions ensures the sum makes sense.
nodes.proof: For a vector x, (A(Bx))ᵢ=Σₗ AᵢₗΣⱼ Bₗⱼxⱼ=Σⱼ(Σₗ AᵢₗBₗⱼ)xⱼ=(ABx)ᵢ. The equality uses rearrangement of finite sums.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Bilinear maps
nodes.summary: A bilinear map is linear in each of two inputs when the other is held fixed.
nodes.detail: Matrix multiplication is bilinear: (A+C)B=AB+CB and A(B+C)=AB+AC, with compatible dimensions. Bilinear does not mean jointly linear.
nodes.proof: For scalars f(x,y)=xy, f(x+x′,y)=xy+x′y and f(x,y+y′)=xy+xy′. But f(2x,2y)=4xy, so treating the pair as one input does not give a linear map.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Counting products in bilinear algorithms
nodes.summary: A bilinear algorithm expresses outputs as combinations of products of linear forms in the inputs.
nodes.detail: Each term multiplies one linear combination of entries of A by one linear combination of entries of B. A tensor records the coefficients. Rank and limiting decompositions are different notions; advanced bounds need more than counting ordinary operations.
nodes.proof: A dot product Σᵢaᵢbᵢ is already a sum of coordinate products. Reusing carefully chosen products can sometimes reduce work in larger bilinear maps. This example establishes neither an optimal rank nor the repository’s exponent bound.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Operation counts and asymptotic growth
nodes.summary: An operation count measures how arithmetic work grows with input size.
nodes.detail: The usual n×n multiplication computes n² entries, each with n multiplications and n−1 additions. This is O(n³) arithmetic operations, ignoring bit lengths.
nodes.proof: There are n³ multiplications and n²(n−1) additions. Their sum is 2n³−n²≤2n³ for n≥1. Thus the school algorithm is O(n³). This is an upper bound, not a lower bound for all algorithms.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: What a matrix multiplication exponent means
nodes.summary: The exponent describes the best asymptotic power for square matrix multiplication in a specified arithmetic model.
nodes.detail: An exponent bound ω≤α allows algorithms with Oε(n^(α+ε)) operations for each ε>0. The infimum need not itself be attained. The catalogue’s stronger claims are not verified here.
nodes.proof: Dividing an n×n product into eight half-size products gives T(n)=8T(n/2)+O(n²). At depth j there are 8ʲ problems of size n/2ʲ; for n=2ᵏ the leaf count is 8ᵏ=n³. Saving recursive products is the motivation, not a proof of a particular improved exponent.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Partial derivatives and the chain rule
nodes.summary: Partial derivatives vary one input while holding the others fixed.
nodes.detail: For differentiable u(t,x) along a differentiable curve x(t), d/dt u(t,x(t))=u_t+x′(t)u_x. In several spatial dimensions use a dot product with the gradient.
nodes.proof: Take u(t,x)=t+x² and x(t)=t². Direct differentiation of t+t⁴ gives 1+4t³. The chain rule gives 1+(2t)(2t²), the same result.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Transport along characteristic curves
nodes.summary: Some PDEs become ODEs when followed along suitable curves.
nodes.detail: For u_t+c u_x=0 with constant c, choose x(t)=x₀+ct. The chain rule gives d/dt u(t,x(t))=0.
nodes.proof: Thus u(t,x₀+ct)=u(0,x₀). Writing x₀=x−ct yields u(t,x)=u₀(x−ct) for differentiable initial data. The nonlinear coupled kinetic system requires additional analysis.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Integrating factors
nodes.summary: Multiplication by a chosen function can turn a first-order equation into a product derivative.
nodes.detail: For y′=ay+b(t), with constant a and continuous b, multiply by e^(−at).
nodes.proof: The product rule gives (e^(−at)y)′=e^(−at)(y′−ay)=e^(−at)b(t). Integrate from 0 to t and multiply by e^(at) to obtain y(t)=e^(at)[y(0)+∫₀ᵗe^(−as)b(s)ds].
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: A basic differential Grönwall estimate
nodes.summary: A differential inequality can bound growth without solving the original equation.
nodes.detail: If E is differentiable, E′≤CE, C is constant, and t≥0, then E(t)≤E(0)e^(Ct).
nodes.proof: Differentiate F=e^(−Ct)E. Then F′=e^(−Ct)(E′−CE)≤0. Hence F(t)≤F(0), which gives the bound. For PDE use, one must first justify the inequality and all differentiations.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: Energy estimates as a method
nodes.summary: Track an integral quantity to control a solution over time.
nodes.detail: Which norm is controlled matters: finite energy alone need not bound all derivatives or guarantee a smooth solution. Boundary behavior and regularity must justify integration by parts.
nodes.proof: Toy example: a smooth periodic solution of u_t=u_xx has E(t)=½∫u² dx. Differentiating and integrating by parts gives E′=∫u u_xx dx=−∫u_x² dx≤0. This is a heat-equation example, not a Vlasov–Maxwell estimate.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning bridge. Level is approximate; the example explains an idea, not the connected research claim. Course links are background reading, not sources for the research proof.

nodes.title: From particle transport to smoothness questions
nodes.summary: A particle distribution is transported by fields that it also helps generate.
nodes.detail: The relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system couples transport in position and momentum with electromagnetic field equations. Global smoothness requires control strong enough to continue the solution; the catalogue’s claimed theorem is not checked here.
nodes.proof: In the simpler free-transport equation f_t+v·∇ₓf=0 with fixed v, f(t,x,v)=f₀(x−tv,v). Differentiating verifies the equation. The actual coupled system adds evolving momentum and fields, so this example supplies intuition only.
